covers.quote: Use a sequential structure for:
instructions – such as how-to guides, recipes and directions
step-by-step content formats – such as forms
reports of events – such as incident reports, histories and case studies.

rules.quote: Use a sequential structure to explain steps or a specific order
rules.violation_condition: Instructions, step-by-step content or an account of events are organised without the sequence needed to follow the steps or order of events.
when: Applies to instructions, including how-to guides, recipes and directions.
Applies to step-by-step content formats, including forms.
Applies to reports of events, including incident reports, histories and case studies.
rules.why: G-2 combines the applicable content types; G-4 consolidates the heading and its restatement.

rules.quote: For example, instructions and transactions are more direct and use the imperative.
rules.violation_condition: An instruction or transactional action is expressed in a non-imperative form instead of directly telling the user what to do.
when: Applies to instructions and transactional actions, not accompanying explanatory statements.
rules.why: G-4 uses the actionable body wording; imperative instructions and past-tense event reporting are different checks.

rules.quote: Reports of events usually use the past tense of the verb.
rules.specification: Treat this as a default for narration of completed events, not a requirement that every verb anywhere in an event report be in the past tense.
rules.violation_condition: An account of a completed event uses a non-past tense where there is no contextual reason to depart from past-tense reporting.
when: Applies to reports of events.
The word ‘usually’ allows contextually appropriate departures from past-tense narration.
rules.why: G-2 retains the qualified scope of ‘usually’; this is distinct from the imperative-mood check.

rules.violation_condition: A webpage title is unclear about the page’s subject or purpose.
rules.why: The title requirement is an independently flaggable textual property, rather than a rule about sequencing.

covers.quote: Start with the most important information – the course selection – so people don’t waste time trying to find it.

rules.quote: Order the content in a sequence that is meaningful for the user.
rules.specification: Assess order against the intended task and its dependencies. In the course-registration example, course selection precedes personal details; do not interpret this as requiring importance order instead of chronological or dependency order in every sequence.
rules.violation_condition: Content is ordered in a way that obstructs the user’s task or makes the sequence difficult to understand.
when: Consider the order in which users need information and make decisions.
In the course-registration example, put course selection before personal details.
rules.why: G-2 treats the course-registration instruction as a specific application of meaningful ordering, not a second ordering finding.

rules.quote: Organise content in a clear order using section headings.
rules.specification: Check for section headings where content needs sectioning. Do not infer that every short page must contain multiple sections; meaningful sequence is checked separately.
rules.violation_condition: Content requiring division into sections lacks section headings that make its organisation apparent.
when: Applies where the content needs division into sections.
rules.why: The grain test separates missing section structure from unclear heading wording and incorrect content order.

rules.quote: Describe the topics or the following section in the headings.
rules.violation_condition: A heading does not describe the topic or section that follows it.
rules.why: The grain test separates a heading’s descriptive accuracy from the requirement to provide section headings.

covers.quote: Create the right number of steps.
Too few steps might mean you have left out important information or grouped too many actions under one heading.
Too many steps might mean you have divided the process into steps so small they are meaningless.
If users need a lot of extra information to do a task, you might have tried to include too much in a single step. You need to break the task into smaller steps.

rules.specification: Assess balance using the stated symptoms: omitted information, too many actions under one heading, excessive explanatory burden within a step, or meaningless subdivisions. The page supplies no numerical step-count or length threshold.
rules.violation_condition: A process has steps that omit important information, crowd too many actions or supporting explanations into one step, or subdivide actions into meaningless fragments.
when: Applies to processes divided into steps.
If users need a lot of extra information for one step, consider whether that step combines too much of the task.
rules.why: G-2 combines symptoms of unsuitable step granularity; G-4 absorbs the repeated instruction to split overloaded steps.

covers.quote: The broad stages can fit into a higher-level sequential structure, or into topics using a hierarchical structure.

rules.quote: If the process is very complex, group steps into broader stages of the process.
rules.specification: The page does not define when a process becomes ‘very complex’. Do not impose a numerical step-count threshold.
rules.violation_condition: A very complex process presents its steps without broader stage groupings.
when: Applies when the process is very complex.
Broader stages may use a higher-level sequential structure or topics in a hierarchical structure.
rules.why: Stage grouping is distinct from step granularity; G-3 records the permitted higher-level structures as options, not separate rules.

rules.quote: If you use a combination of structures, design menu and link items based on how users find their way through the content.
rules.specification: Assessment requires an account of users’ intended routes through the content. The page does not specify a menu arrangement or link-label pattern that can be assumed universally.
rules.violation_condition: Menu and link items in content combining structures do not support the routes users need to find their way through that content.
when: Applies when content combines structures.
rules.why: This is a conditional requirement for navigation organisation, distinct from heading consistency.

rules.quote: Be consistent in the language, style and design of headings at the same level across the content.
rules.violation_condition: Headings at the same level use inconsistent language, style or design across the content.
when: In this passage, the requirement applies to content combining structures.
Compare headings at the same level.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the dimensions of same-level heading consistency together as one consistency check.

covers.quote: For instructional and transactional content, people want to know what they need to do. They don’t need long explanations of the process.

rules.quote: Write clear instructions users can follow
rules.specification: Read the heading through its immediate explanation: required actions should be apparent, and explanations should be limited to what users need. Necessary explanations are allowed; no numerical length limit is stated.
rules.violation_condition: Instructional or transactional content obscures what users need to do with unnecessary or lengthy explanations of the process.
when: Applies to instructional and transactional content.
Explanations may be included when users need them.
rules.why: G-4 reads the heading with its explanatory body; G-2 allows necessary explanations, while overloaded step granularity is checked separately.
